title: Xerox Punk — Ransom Zine Manifesto
description: A punk-flyer template built on deliberate misalignment, ransom-note type rotation, and halftone photocopy noise — the slide equivalent of a seventh-generation xerox pinned to a telephone pole. Tape-mark corner anchors and torn-edge cuts separate it from cleaner brutalist siblings in the same category.
philosophy: This template treats imperfection as ideology. It borrows from the Jamie Reid cut-and-paste tradition — where graphic violence and urgency are inseparable — because a perfectly kerned slide cannot communicate crisis or rebellion. It refuses every softening gesture: no gradients, no shadows, no radius, no breathing room it didn't earn. It is built for speakers who need the room to feel friction before a single word is spoken, and for audiences who distrust anything that looks designed by committee.
goodFor: Hackathon kickoff title cards demanding immediate high-energy impact
Counter-culture or activist talk openers where polish would undermine credibility
3-line pull quotes that need to feel urgent, handmade, and non-negotiable
DIY or underground event announcements requiring deliberate visual noise
avoidFor: Chart-heavy quarterly business reviews or data-dense financial decks
Formal investor pitches or regulated-industry boardroom presentations
Multi-column body copy slides where legibility is non-negotiable
Brand system presentations requiring consistent alignment and typographic hierarchy
author: harness

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel like a photocopied flyer peeled off a telephone pole after a week of rain — urgent, abrasive, assembled by someone with no patience for beauty. Compositional tension lives in deliberate misalignment: headline and subtitle refuse to share an axis, each block staking its own territory. Halftone grain and xerox degradation are not decorative effects but load-bearing texture. The mood is confrontational and unmediated — the visual equivalent of a shout, not a presentation.

examples.layoutNotes: Full-bleed composition with no governing grid — the title block is slammed into the upper-left quadrant at a deliberate counter-clockwise tilt, as if cut and paste-mounted by hand. Subtitle or deck descriptor occupies the lower-right zone, rotated clockwise, spatially and angularly disconnected from the title. Tape-mark graphic anchors pin all four corners as the sole framing device, replacing any margin or border system. A halftone noise field bleeds edge-to-edge beneath all type, bisected by a rough torn-edge horizontal rule near the vertical midpoint.

examples.promptCore: The slide should feel assembled with scissors and rubber cement at 3am — each text block reads as if cut from a different source document and taped to a photocopy backing crawling with grain and halftone artifact. Compositional rhythm is deliberately unresolved: tension between the heavy anchor of the primary statement and the skittering placement of the secondary fragment creates visual friction before the audience reads a word. Inspired by Jamie Reid's ransom collage tradition — urgency and ideological weight are inseparable from imperfection. Avoid any softening: no unified visual system, no calming negative space that wasn't earned through collision.

examples.layoutNotes: Broken 12-col grid where content blocks deliberately breach column boundaries — a pull-quote fragment occupies cols 1-8 at a slight negative rotation while an attribution or secondary callout is pinned hard to the lower-right, cols 9-12, counter-rotated. Tape-mark corner anchors appear at upper-left and lower-right to visually 'hold' the composition in place. A torn horizontal rule (not a clean line) divides the primary statement from the secondary fragment, with halftone noise texture layered across the full bleed background. Page marker sits bottom-left, outside the main content zone, mimicking a zine page stamp.
